title: Real data, real map - Grand atlas strategy for my kid (and me)
author: walm00
selftext:
I love strategy games. I've played a ton of Civilization, Warcraft, StarCraft, Age of Empires, you name it :) Even Ages of Conflict and some of the world-map games on Roblox.

My son loves those map games as well, but the ones he found were all about clicking fast or way too complicated (and/or looking lame). So I started making one for us. It's called TEOLANDS. You pick a real country and try to grow it with economy, diplomacy and armies.

I built it assisting with Claude Code and Codex. I'd already made 3 games, and I had my own context setup and a delivery desk plugin for running several developing sessions at once, so this time it was much faster. The logic, the mechanics and what stays in come from me and from playing it with my son.

Balance was one hard part. With real numbers, small countries disappear fast. Protect them too much and the world stops feeling real. Latvia, where I'm from, can survive and matter, but it doesn't get to own the map.

The other was/is performance. The game runs 10 ticks a second across 218 countries and 2,404 regions, with armies, money, diplomacy and construction all changing, and all of it has to save properly and stay in sync over LAN. (Good thing I have a powerful workstation, because I can run all 10 LAN players on it and simulate games.)

I've signed up on Steam and I'm waiting to be approved so I can publish. Meanwhile I put up a web demo with six countries and three game years: [https://teolands.com/](https://demo.teolands.com/)

If anyone wants to test the full game on desktop or over LAN, you can apply there as well.

Any feedback welcome.  
I will share more specific details about the build, and tool/tech-stack and tips and tricks in a separate post. This is more about the demo / game itself.  
And if you've launched on Steam, I'd really appreciate any tips and tricks.

comments.author: biggdogg420
comments.body: Latvia sounds like a good balance test. Could you give a small country one goal it can reach through diplomacy, like assembling a defensive coalition that lasts the three demo years? That would make a successful small-country run visible without having to make it good at conquest.

replies.author: walm00
replies.body:
That's a good idea! Latvia in the demo already kind of plays like that. It's the hard pick, and the plan is basically survive, find friends, then grow. But right now holding on with good allies doesn't count as a win.

In the version I'm working on, I'm testing a Grand Project as the last step of a Prosperity win. Once you start it, the other countries get warned and come after you, so you'd better be ready. It's brutal for small countries though. Latvia hasn't survived it in my test games yet :D

So a goal like "keep your coalition alive until the end" could be a better path for a small country. Going on my list.

comments.author: walm00
comments.body:
For anyone interested about the performance side: the game runs 10 ticks a second, so at normal speed each tick has 100 ms to finish. At 4x speed that drops to 25 ms.

A late-game tick was taking 41.7 ms. Fine at normal speed, but at 4x the game couldn't keep up and clicks started to lag. It's now 12.4 ms, so 4x fits with time to spare. That spare time matters, because the host also has to update every LAN player and autosave. All 10 players at 4x is still too heavy, so I'm not done.   
The risky part of optimizing a simulation is quietly changing the rules, so I hashed the whole world state at 56 checkpoints before and after. All 56 had to match exactly. Most of the waste was expensive work hiding inside loops, like computer players rebuilding the whole economy for every upgrade they considered.

I'll write up the full method in a separate post.
